BERT4Rec’s original paper explicitly identifies the mismatch between random masked-item reconstruction and next-item prediction. It trains on randomly masked positions, additionally generates examples masking only the final item, and appends a reserved mask token at inference, reading that token’s final hidden representation. Its single-mask ablation is not a terminal-only versus random-mask comparison; it does not establish an optimal terminal-mask proportion. Reported attention toward recent items is evidence of recency use, not proof of a shortcut. Bidirectional training with visible shifted targets would leak answers. [BERT4Rec paper](https://arxiv.org/html/1904.06690)

“Does It Look Sequential?” (RecSys 2024) evaluates frozen SASRec and GRU4Rec models on original versus shuffled histories, excluding held-out targets from shuffling. It measures HR@10/NDCG@10 degradation and top-10 Jaccard overlap, finding weak sequential structure in several popular datasets. These are model-dependent diagnostics, not direct evidence about BERT4Rec or the four requested categories. [Paper](https://arxiv.org/html/2408.12008)

Suggested adaptation: freeze each category’s BERT4Rec and compare original histories, fully shuffled histories, and histories shuffled while preserving the latest item. Keep padding and appended mask fixed; permute only historical item positions. Report paired validation HR@10 changes and Jaccard@10, with uncertainty. Preserving the latest item helps distinguish earlier-order sensitivity from reliance on immediate recency; adding a last-item-only input probe measures dependence on broader context. These extensions are diagnostic proposals, not findings from the cited papers. Sensitivity alone does not establish useful sequence reasoning, and invariance does not prove a shortcut. Keep all perturbations diagnostic; retain the host’s unchanged macro validation HR@10 for selection and one trained checkpoint per category.
